hypotheses: D is a PROPER decreasing family on a finite ground set X, containing the empty set and every singleton. Properness matters: the case D = 2^X is separated explicitly and handled by the remark that there are then no obstructions and one colour with the empty generator FAMILY costs zero.

H, the inclusion-minimal forbidden family, is nonempty and every member has size at least two. This is a consequence of every singleton being good, and it is the exact step that makes the sufficiency construction work.

alpha(D) = min { max over U in D of w(U) : w_i >= 0 and w(e) >= 1 for every e in H }. H constraints suffice by monotonicity; the minimum is attained because clipping each coordinate at one keeps feasibility and cannot raise any good-set weight, so the search may be restricted to the compact cube [0,1]^X. Irrelevant coordinates are permitted.

A P14 scalar sandwich of width kappa means: 0 <= a_i < 1 for every i; a(U) < 1 implies U in D; and U in D implies a(U) < kappa. Both implications are SETWISE, quantified over every U contained in X, not over a sampled family and not in expectation.
kappa >= 1 throughout (A1). This is why the infimum admissible width is max(1, alpha) and not alpha.
In the (A3) dual, mu is supported on sets that really are forbidden in the ORIGINAL family and nu on sets that really are good, with the nu weights summing to one.
For the (A2) rounding, beta is the good-set maximum of an EXPLICIT rational feasible w, not of an unknown optimum; the formula is then K = max(408, floor(408 beta) + 1).
reconstruction:
I rebuilt the three sections from the read bytes and then recomputed every numerical claim.

A1, necessity. Suppose a is a sandwich of width kappa. The contrapositive of 'a(U) < 1 implies U in D' is that every forbidden U has a(U) >= 1, so a is feasible for the alpha programme; a is nonnegative by hypothesis. D is finite, so max over good U of a(U) is attained and is strictly below kappa. Since alpha is a minimum over feasible vectors, alpha <= that maximum < kappa. Hence a sandwich forces kappa > alpha.

A1, sufficiency. Take an optimal w and clip it at one; clipping is safe because for a forbidden e either some coordinate of e already carries w_i >= 1, in which case the clipped sum is at least one on that coordinate alone, or every coordinate of e is below one and clipping is the identity on e. The clipped vector is still optimal because clipping cannot raise a good-set weight. Two cases. If alpha < 1 and kappa = 1, every singleton is good, so w_i = w({i}) <= alpha < 1, and a = w is already a sandwich. Otherwise kappa > 1, since kappa >= 1 and kappa > alpha. Put a_i = (1-theta) w_i + theta/2 with theta in (0,1). Then a_i <= 1 - theta/2 < 1. On a forbidden e, a(e) = (1-theta) w(e) + theta |e| / 2 >= (1-theta) + theta = 1, and this is exactly where |e| >= 2 is spent. On a good U, a(U) <= (1-theta) alpha + theta |X| / 2, which tends to alpha < kappa as theta falls, so a small enough theta finishes it. I confirmed the interval arithmetic of the A2 instantiation: with beta >= 1, K = floor(408 beta) + 1, kappa = K/408 and theta = (kappa - beta)/(|X| + 1), one gets 0 < kappa - beta <= 1/408, hence theta <= 1/(408(|X|+1)) < 1, and beta + theta |X| / 2 < kappa reduces to |X| / (2(|X|+1)) < 1, which is true. The stronger form beta + theta|X|/2 implies the needed (1-theta)beta + theta|X|/2 because beta >= 0.

A2, weak duality. For any feasible w, sum(mu) <= sum_e mu_e w(e) since each w(e) >= 1 on the forbidden support; then sum_e mu_e w(e) = sum_i w_i sum_{e contains i} mu_e <= sum_i w_i sum_{U contains i} nu_U, using w_i >= 0 and the (A3) coordinate inequality; and that equals sum_U nu_U w(U) <= max over good U of w(U) because nu is a probability distribution on good sets. Minimising over w gives sum(mu) <= alpha. No strong-duality theorem and no solver status is used.

A3, the three examples. For the independent sets of K(m,m) the good family is 2^A union 2^B and the minimal forbidden sets are the m^2 crossing pairs. Primal w = 1/2 everywhere gives objective m/2; the dual takes a perfect matching at 1/2 per edge and nu = 1/2 on each side, whose coordinate loads are 1/2 on both sides, matching exactly. For the complete r-uniform forbidden family, uniform 1/r gives objective (r-1)/r; the uniform r-set and (r-1)-set distributions both put load (r-1)/n on each coordinate, which I computed from C(n-1,r-1)/C(n,r) = r/n and C(n-1,r-2)/C(n,r-1) = (r-1)/n. For the third example I rebuilt the shape the sentence describes - two permitted complementary tail sets and two forbidden complementary tail sets - as a four-coordinate family and confirmed alpha = 1 by exact LP, hence K = floor(408) + 1 = 409 from (A2), which is the number the object reports.

Cross-check of 408 itself: P14-A section 1 sets R = ceil(12 A^2) + 2 and K = ceil(8 kappa (R+1)); at A = 2 this is R = 50 and K = ceil(408 kappa). The constant is inherited, not invented here.
